title: Holy days and the saints' calendar
hook: a few great feasts are kept like Sundays (the list varies by country)
tomorrow: Camp 3 close: a rule of life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifty days of Easter, and the alleluia coming back. Your line was longer than lent. Did you keep one celebration going? A new week, and the last full lesson of this camp. Day one hundred fifty-five.

Open a Catholic calendar, the kind that hangs in a parish hall, and look at any square. There's a name in it. March 19, Joseph. August 15, Mary taken up into heaven. November 1, all the saints at once. Then a random Tuesday in July, and there's still a name: some bishop, some farmer's daughter, some martyr from a city you've never heard of. Almost no day is empty. And a few of the squares carry a special mark, because on those days Catholics are asked to go to Mass, even on a Wednesday.
screen: `A NAME IN EVERY SQUARE.` → `A FEW SPECIALLY MARKED.`

segments.voice: Those marked days are holy days of obligation. Catholics are asked to go to Mass every Sunday, and on a handful of great feasts they're asked to do the same, whatever day of the week it falls on, and to rest from unnecessary work where they can. The Church's general law lists ten of these feasts, among them Christmas, the Epiphany, the Ascension, Mary the Mother of God, the Assumption, Saint Joseph, Peter and Paul, and All Saints. But it lets each country's bishops trim the list or move a feast to the nearest Sunday. So the list really does vary. In the United States the list is shorter, and some are lifted when they fall right next to a weekend. Ask a Catholic in Ireland or Italy and you'll get a different answer. Then there's everyone else on the calendar. The saints' days. The Church keeps a general calendar of saints for the whole world, and a much longer book, the Roman Martyrology, which lists saints and martyrs for every day of the year, often several on a single day. Here's the surprising part: a saint's feast is usually kept on the day they died, not the day they were born. The old Latin name for that day is dies natalis, birthday, because the Church thinks of it as their birthday into heaven. So every morning, somewhere, somebody is keeping a birthday for someone who died a long time ago. Parishes are named for them. Children are named for them. And in some Catholic families, a name day is kept like a second birthday.
screen: `MARKED DAYS: KEPT LIKE A SUNDAY.` · `THE LIST VARIES BY COUNTRY.` · `A SAINT FOR EVERY DAY.` · `THE DAY THEY DIED: A BIRTHDAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find today's saint. After the bell, look it up on any Catholic calendar, and pick one name. For now, settle and breathe, and think about the idea itself: that today already belongs to someone who lived a whole life and finished it. Think, too, of someone you knew who has died. What day was theirs? If you pray, you can ask today's saint to pray for you, or for them. If you don't, simply remember one life with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Dies natalis. Latin for birthday, the day a saint died, kept as their birthday into heaven. Today's word.
Your line: every day belongs to someone. Today, find out whose day it is, and say their name once, to yourself or to someone else. Day one hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics go to Mass on Sundays and on their country's holy days of obligation, such as Christmas and All Saints; many also follow the saints' calendar, keeping name days, the feasts of their parish's patron and their own patron saints.

fork.setup: it's a Wednesday, and your parish calendar marks today with a special symbol. what are Catholics asked to do?
options: go to Mass, as on a Sunday.
nothing: red just marks a saint's day.
fork.reveal: that mark means a holy day of obligation. Catholics are asked to go to Mass and rest where they can, whatever day of the week it falls on.

original.note: Latin: birthday. the Church's name for the day a saint died, their birthday into heaven.

trapdoor: what you thought: a holy day of obligation is a rule about extra Masses.
what it means: a great feast kept like a Sunday, with Mass and rest, on a list that varies by country.
what a scholar hears: the universal law (canon 1246) lists ten such feasts, and each bishops' conference may suppress some or move them to Sunday.

notes: Canon 1246 §1 lists: Nativity, Epiphany, Ascension, Body and Blood of Christ, Holy Mary Mother of God, Immaculate Conception, Assumption, Saint Joseph, Saints Peter and Paul, All Saints. The script names a selection. Confirm.

United States: six holy days (Mary Mother of God, Ascension in some provinces, Assumption, All Saints, Immaculate Conception, Christmas); obligation abrogated for some when they fall on a Saturday or Monday. The script says 'some of them are lifted'. Confirm.
Canon 1247: obligation to participate in Mass and abstain from work that hinders worship and rest. Paraphrased.
Feast on the day of death (dies natalis) is the usual rule, with exceptions (e.g. Nativity of John the Baptist, of Mary). Hedged with 'usually'.
Roman Martyrology count per day ('often a dozen or more'): confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): calendars do not reliably print holy days of obligation in red (red often marks martyrs or feasts), so hook, teach, screens and fork now say 'specially marked'; cut the uncited US count (six) and Martyrology count (a dozen or more); softened the 'for many Catholics' name-day claim.
